summary: Describes the Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate Management Protocols, which cover how certificates are requested, issued, renewed and revoked between users and certification authorities. It was replaced by RFC 4210.

plainLanguage.summary: A digital ID card has to be handed out, renewed and cancelled somehow. This document sets the rules for those conversations between a person and the office that issues the cards.

questions: how are x.509 certificates requested and issued
what is the certificate management protocol
what is proof of possession in pki
subtitle: How certificate authorities, registration authorities and end entities request, issue, update and revoke X.509 certificates.

tldr.problem: Certificates have to be requested, issued, renewed, recovered and revoked, and a public key infrastructure needs one agreed set of messages for each of those steps.
tldr.mechanism: Every exchange is a PKIMessage with a header, a typed body and optional protection, carried over files, a simple TCP protocol, e-mail or HTTP. An end entity proves it holds the private key, and the CA keeps final say over what the certificate contains.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2510 was a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 4210.

today: RFC 2510 was a Proposed Standard published in March 1999 and has been obsoleted by RFC 4210, which is the specification to use now.

sections.title: PKI Management and Its Players
sections.content:
RFC 2510 defines the Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) Certificate Management Protocols. It says management protocols are REQUIRED to support on-line interactions between PKI components, for example between a Certification Authority (CA) and a client, or between two CAs that issue cross-certificates for each other.

Three kinds of entity appear. An end entity is the subject named in a certificate, and may be a person or an application. The CA is the entity named as issuer. A Registration Authority (RA) is an optional extra component that can handle things like personal authentication, token distribution, revocation reporting and key generation. When no RA is present, the CA is assumed to do its work, so the protocol looks the same to the end entity.

The operations covered include CA establishment, end entity initialization, initial registration and certification, key pair update, certificate update, CA key update, cross-certification, key pair recovery and revocation requests.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a person who needs an ID card, an office that makes the cards, and sometimes a helper desk that checks who you are before the office makes it.

sections.title: Design Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC lists thirteen requirements. Among them: it must be possible to update any key pair without affecting any other, confidentiality should be kept to a minimum to ease regulatory problems, and different industry-standard algorithms (the text names RSA, DSA, MD5 and SHA-1) must be usable. Key pairs may be generated by the end entity, an RA or a CA, and the protocols must work over transports such as mail, http, TCP/IP and ftp.

A key rule is that final authority for certificate creation rests with the CA. A CA may change field values or extensions according to its policy, for example by shortening the requested validity period, so every entity must cope with a certificate that differs from the one requested. The protocols must also support a graceful, scheduled change from one CA key pair to the next.
sections.plainLanguage: The office has the last word on what goes on your ID card, even if you asked for something slightly different.

sections.title: Registration and Proof of Possession
sections.content:
Initial registration schemes are classified by where it starts, whether the end entity's messages are authenticated, where the key is generated, and whether the end entity confirms receipt. Authentication relies on an initial authentication key and a reference value, which the CA or RA hands over out of band. Conforming CA, RA and end entity equipment MUST support the centralized scheme: it starts at the CA, which also generates the key, with no on-line authentication and no confirmation, so the single message from the CA carries the whole Personal Security Environment.

In the basic authenticated scheme, the end entity generates the key, creates a request protected by the initial authentication key, and later sends a confirmation. If verifying that confirmation fails, the RA or CA MUST revoke the new certificate if it has been published or made available.

CAs and RAs MUST enforce proof of possession of the private key by some means. A signature key can sign a value. An encryption key can be handed over, or the end entity can decrypt a challenge, directly or indirectly. The RFC encourages the indirect method, where the certificate is issued encrypted and the confirmation shows it was decrypted, because it needs no extra messages.
sections.plainLanguage: To get your card you have to show you really own the secret key, a bit like proving you own a lock by opening it in front of the clerk.

sections.title: The PKIMessage Structure
sections.content:
Every management message is a PKIMessage, defined in ASN.1, with four parts: a PKIHeader, a PKIBody, an optional PKIProtection and optional extraCerts that help the recipient verify certificates.

The header names the sender and recipient and can carry a message time, the protection algorithm, key identifiers, a transactionID that stays the same across request, response and confirmation, and sender and recipient nonces for replay protection. The body is one of 24 choices: initialization, certification, key update, key recovery, revocation and cross-certification requests with matching responses, plus a PKCS #10 request, challenge and response messages, announcements, confirmation, nested, general and error messages. Protection is a bit string computed over the DER encoding of the header and body.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message is an envelope with an address label, a letter inside, and maybe a wax seal to show nobody changed it.

sections.title: Transport Options
sections.content:
The RFC defines four ways to carry PKI messages. In the file-based option, a file MUST contain only the DER encoding of one PKI message. In the e-mail and HTTP options, the message travels as a MIME object of type application/pkixcmp, base64 encoded for mail.

The direct TCP-based protocol uses well-defined port 829. Each message is a 32-bit length, an 8-bit flag and a value. An initiator can send a request and receive either the response or a polling reference and a time to check back, then poll until the final message arrives. Confirmations are sent as a message answered by a negative poll response.
sections.plainLanguage: The same letter can go by post, by email, by web, or over a direct phone line. The phone line also lets you call back later to ask if your answer is ready.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that the whole memo is about security mechanisms, then spells out one cryptographic risk. When an end entity must prove it holds a decryption key, it is effectively challenged to decrypt something, such as its own certificate. That scheme could be vulnerable if the key holder could be fooled into decrypting an arbitrary challenge and returning the plaintext to an attacker.

The RFC says other failures would be needed for this to work against the specified protocol, but future services such as notary or trusted time could be exposed. Implementations should be very careful about decrypting arbitrary ciphertext and revealing the result.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not open any sealed note a stranger hands you and read the answer back to them, because it might be a trick.
